newsitem.title: FRANCE: French economy faces more chaos after talks fail.
newsitem.headline: French economy faces more chaos after talks fail.

text.p: France's economy faced a further battering on Thursday after the breakdown of government-mediated talks between striking truck drivers and employers to end an 11-day dispute over pay and working conditions.
The truckers vowed to maintain their blockades on main roads and at key industrial sites after trade union officials announced the breakdown and said the government had ended its mediation efforts.
"(Government representative) Mr Roger Cros decided to put an end to his mediation mission," Roger Politti, secretary-general of the Force Ouvriere union, told reporters.
Union sources said the breakdown was over pay. Truckers have demanded a pay rise of up to 23 percent but employers have offered only one percent.
"Unfortunately, we must maintain our blockades," Politti said.
The truckers have set up about 250 roadblocks around the country which have started to strangle the French economy.
Cros, who met Transport Minister Bernard Pons after the talks broke down, said he viewed his mediation as a success "because all the points that were on the agenda were discussed".
Pons told reporters he also felt Cros had been successful.
"Under these conditions, I would not understand it if the roads continued to be blocked," said Pons.
There was no immediate official explanation whether the minister's comments were meant as a veiled threat that the government was about to use police to try to clear the roads.
Jehan de Marne, representing the employers, blamed union representatives for the breakdown.
"The sticking point is that our negotiating partners will not acccept or recognise the positive character of our proposals," he said.
The two sides agreed however to meet on Friday to sign a deal on some issues, mostly about pension rights, which had been resolved on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government has worked overtime to try to broker a deal to end the strike.
Force Ouvriere and the Communist-led CGT union led a 24-day wave of anti-government strikes that virtually paralysed France in late 1995.
Sudden snow and sleet in several areas of northern and eastern France, including some Paris suburbs, brought new misery to motorists trying to find a way around the truckers' blockades.
Barricades around petrol depots and 12 of 13 refineries across France have closed up to 2,000 of the country's 18,000 petrol stations.
Petrol rationing was imposed in some areas so supplies could be maintained for fire engines and ambulances.
Tempers flared when frustrated motorists saw official cars drive up to petrol stations and receive precious fuel while they were denied supplies, witnesses said.
Police were called to several petrol stations where irate motorists refused to allow emergency vehicles, including doctors' cars, to jump queues.
The roadblocks have forced the closure of some factories and cut supplies of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit.
School buses stopped running in the southeastern Drome department because of lack of fuel.
Farmers reported shortages of animal feed as grain shipments were hit. The strike was also disrupting mail deliveries.

In a 20-hour overnight negotiating session which ended early on Wednesday, union and government officials said progress had been made on two of the truckers' key demands -- retirement at 55 instead of 60 and shorter working hours.
The strike and a parallel one in Denmark caused problems in other European countries, clogging highways and ports and disrupting commerce.

Thousands of truck drivers from Britain, Spain, Germany and other countries were trapped by the blockades without enough food or money. Growing tensions led to some violent confrontations with French truckers.
British Transport Secretary Sir George Young pleaded on Wednesday for the release of British drivers blockaded in France by the striking French truckers.
In a letter to Pons, Young said the British drivers were innocent victims of the dispute.
"British drivers have nothing to do with this dispute, and there is a growing sense of anger in Britain that so many still remain trapped," said Young.
